title: Spend vectors wisely
brief: Twenty million chunks, a memory quota that is already tight, a mix of languages and an embedding model that will be retired within years. Choose the model, the dimensions and the compression, and say how you would prove recall held.

blocks.md: Embedding choices are storage and quality choices at once. Topics `w04-t12` (model choice), `w04-t13` (dimensions and Matryoshka), `w04-t14` (quantization and rescoring) and `w04-t15` (asymmetric prompts, multilingual, drift) cover the mechanisms. A leaderboard is only a shortlist: MTEB found no method that wins every task, and MMTEB extends the benchmark to more than 500 tasks [[r17]] [[r18]]. Start by sizing the raw vectors, because in Azure AI Search the vector quota is a memory quota and HNSW adds 1% to 20% on top of float32 vectors [[r36]].

blocks.title: Raw vector memory
blocks.expr: bytes = vectors x dimensions x bytes_per_dimension

vars.v: chunk count, one vector per chunk (more if you keep several fields)
model default or the shortened value you configure
4 for float32, 2 for float16, 1 for int8, 0.125 for binary

blocks.example: 20,000,000 vectors at 1,536 dimensions in float32 is 20,000,000 x 1,536 x 4, about **122.9 GB** before index overhead. As int8 it is about 30.7 GB, and binary is about 3.8 GB plus any full-precision copies you keep for rescoring.

blocks.title: Pick a compression setup
blocks.prompt: Flip the constraints. Note how recall tolerance and native dimensions change the answer.

values.label: A point or two of recall is fine

options.name: Full precision
options.summary: Keep float32 or float16 vectors at their native size.

options.name: Scalar quantization (int8)
options.summary: Store each dimension as an 8-bit integer.

options.name: Binary quantization with rescoring
options.summary: One bit per dimension, with oversampling and rescoring from the originals.

options.name: Matryoshka truncation plus scalar
options.summary: Keep only the leading dimensions of a Matryoshka-trained model, then quantize.

options.name: Truncation plus binary, originals discarded
options.summary: The smallest index: truncated, binary, and `stored: false` for the full vector.

ok.why: No loss and the simplest setup, so keep it while the quota allows.

tight.why: It is the biggest index, and the quota is the constraint.

critical.why: Nothing to lose, and it is your baseline for measuring every other option.

loose.why: You are paying for recall you said you do not need.

low.why: Vectors are already small, so compression saves little.

high.why: 3,072 dimensions in float32 is 12,288 bytes per vector.

ok.why: Works, but you take a small loss for savings you do not need.

tight.why: 4 times smaller, and about 99.3% of float32 performance in an open benchmark [[r22]].

critical.why: The loss is small and measurable against the full-precision baseline.

low.why: The saving is smaller in absolute terms.

high.why: A 4 times cut on large vectors is worth taking.

ok.why: More machinery than you need, and it depends on oversampling and rescoring [[r21]].

tight.why: 32 times smaller in the open benchmark (AI Search says up to 28 times) [[r21]] [[r22]].

critical.why: About 96% retained with rescoring and about 92.5% without, so measure first [[r22]].

loose.why: Rescoring recovers most of the recall for a large saving.

low.why: Binary suits dimensions above 1,024 and embeddings centred on zero [[r21]].

high.why: This is the case it is best for [[r21]].

tight.why: Stacks two savings, but needs a Matryoshka-trained model, quantization and a new field [[r20]].

critical.why: Test it: a 256-dimension 3-large vector still beat full ada-002 on MTEB, though your data may differ [[r12]].

low.why: There is little to truncate from a small vector.

high.why: Large Matryoshka vectors such as 3-large (3,072) are what truncation is for [[r12]].

ok.why: It is irreversible overkill when the quota is comfortable.

tight.why: The largest size cut, but `stored: false` means a partial document update loses the vector unless you resend it [[r20]].

critical.why: Discarding the originals removes your rescoring and your rollback.

loose.why: Acceptable when recall has slack and you re-send full vectors on updates.

low.why: Truncation and binary both suit large vectors.

high.why: Large native vectors give the cuts room to work.

blocks.takeaway: Compress when the quota or cost is the bottleneck, keep the originals when recall is critical, and always measure recall against an uncompressed baseline on your own queries.

items.symptom: Recall fell after shortening vectors by hand
items.cause: The model was not Matryoshka-trained, or the truncated vector was not re-normalised [[r12]] [[r19]].
items.fix: Use the `dimensions` parameter or a trained model, and re-normalise a hand-truncated vector.

items.symptom: An open model scores well in the benchmark and poorly in the app
items.cause: The query and passage prefixes were left out on one or both sides [[r16]].
items.fix: Apply the model card's prefixes on both sides and assert them in a test.

items.symptom: Partial document updates wipe the vectors
items.cause: Binary plus Matryoshka with `stored: false` discards the full vector, so a partial update loses it unless you resend it [[r20]].
items.fix: Send the full vector on every update, or keep originals.

items.symptom: Results turn to nonsense after a model swap
items.cause: Vectors from different models are not comparable, and Azure says embeddings cannot be upgraded in place [[r13]].
items.fix: Build a new field or index for the new model and cut over by alias (see `w03-l3`).

blocks.title: Dates and limits to check, 2026-10-13
blocks.md: The Azure retirement schedule (updated 2026-09-21) lists text-embedding-3-large, 3-small and ada-002 as retiring 2028-02-09, while an older page had ada-002 at no earlier than April 30, 2026, so read the live schedule [[r14]]. The embedding input limit is 8,192 tokens in the Azure model table and OpenAI docs, and 8,191 on the AI Search chunking page, so stay a little under [[r1]] [[r13]].

quiz.q: How many gigabytes do 20,000,000 float32 vectors of 1,536 dimensions need before any index overhead?
quiz.hint: A float32 value is 4 bytes. Use 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes.
quiz.explain: 20,000,000 x 1,536 x 4 bytes is 122,880,000,000 bytes, about 122.9 GB. HNSW adds 1% to 20% on top, and the AI Search vector quota is a memory quota, so this is the figure to compare with the quota. int8 cuts it to about 30.7 GB [[r36]].

quiz.q: A self-hosted E5 model scores well in the benchmark but retrieval in the app is mediocre, with no errors anywhere. What is the most likely cause?
options: The `query: ` and `passage: ` prefixes were never added
The vectors were stored as float32 instead of int8
The HNSW `m` value is below its documented default
The embedding input limit of 8,192 tokens was exceeded for every chunk
quiz.explain: E5 requires the prefixes, and leaving them out silently lowers quality, which matches a benchmark gap with no error. Storing float32 is the higher-quality choice, an `m` change shifts recall only slightly, and exceeding the input limit would raise errors or truncation on every chunk rather than mediocre results [[r16]].

quiz.q: Select the true statements about quantization and truncation in Azure AI Search.
options: Rescoring works only with HNSW, and `defaultOversampling` defaults to 4
`truncationDimension` needs scalar or binary quantization, and cannot be added to an existing field
You can switch an existing vector field to quantized vectors in place
`discardOriginals` is available for binary quantization only
quiz.explain: Rescoring, the oversampling default, the truncation prerequisites and the binary-only discard option are documented. A quantized field needs a new vector profile and a new field, so in-place switching is false, which is why quantization is planned like a re-index [[r20]] [[r21]].

quiz.q: The corpus is mostly German and Hindi. MTEB averages are 62.3 for 3-small and 64.6 for 3-large, and the cost difference is small. What do you do?
options: Stay on 3-small, because a 2.3 point MTEB gap is negligible for any corpus
Move to ada-002, which costs less per page and has fixed 1,536 dimensions
Test 3-large first, shortened with `dimensions` if memory requires
Apply binary quantization to close the language gap with the cheaper model
quiz.explain: MIRACL, a multilingual retrieval benchmark, averages 44.0 for 3-small and 54.9 for 3-large, a far wider gap than MTEB shows, and ada-002 scores 31.4. Shortening 3-large with `dimensions` recovers memory. Quantization trades recall for size and cannot add language skill [[r12]] [[r13]].

takeaways: Size raw vectors first: vectors x dimensions x 4 bytes, plus 1% to 20% for HNSW, against a memory quota
A leaderboard is a shortlist: no model wins every MTEB task, and MIRACL shows what an average hides for other languages
Compress when memory is the bottleneck, keep originals for rescoring, and plan quantization like a re-index
Apply the model's query and document prefixes, and check the retirement date before committing
